newsitem.title: CHINA: Sino-German venture opens Shanghai wholesale store.
newsitem.headline: Sino-German venture opens Shanghai wholesale store.

text.p: A Sino-German joint venture has opened Shanghai's first wholesale superstore and plans to launch four more in the East China region next year, a company official said on Monday.
"This is the first Cash and Carry store of its kind in Shanghai," said Willi Rasch, general manager of Metro Jinjiang Shopping Centre Co Ltd.
"Cash and Carry is a new idea in China. We are low cost, big stock and low price, with everything under one roof," he added.
Wholesale cash and carry stores don't give credit and customers are expected to arrange for transport themselves.
Metro Jinjiang is a joint venture between Germany's Metro International Management GmbH and the Jinjiang Group of Shanghai, with the German partner holding 60 percent equity.
Rasch said the superstore was only open to businesses with a membership card, for which they need to show a business licence and an identity card. It is not open to individuals.

The store offers about 6,450 food items and 8,500 non-food products, including electronic goods, office stationery, sports equipment, bicycles, household daily items and food, all on a wholesale consignment basis.
Rasch said only 10-15 percent of the goods on offer are imported and the rest made in China.
The superstore, with a shopping area of 8,900 square metres (95,764 sq ft), has attracted 4,500-5,500 customers a day since it opened on October 31.
Rasch said customers were mainly smaller, family-run stores, restaurants, hotels, offices and factory canteens. The superstore is open from 3 a.m., when clients come to buy fresh food, until 10 p.m.
One foreign analyst said the superstore would appeal to smaller businesses that pay cash for goods but not to larger, specialised stores that needed a wider choice and could obtain goods on credit.
Shanghai has many specialised wholesalers but none offer as wide a range of products as the new superstore.
Rasch said the joint venture planned to open a second store in Shanghai and others in the east China cities of Wuxi, Nanjing and Hefei next year.
Each of the superstores will involve an investment of $25 million to $30 million. All but the Hefei store have already been officially approved, he said.
Rasch declined to give turnover figures or targets and said it was too early to say when the venture would turn a profit.
"A wholesale business needs a lot of investment and the payback is longer than for a normal store," he said.
City officials have said they welcome large-scale and specialised investment in retail facilities to diversify and upgrade Shanghai's commercial base and bring it closer to international standards.
